description: Solo team for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. We are building Sol Shift, a browser game for kids ages 7 to 12: run a Mars base for 30 sols, balance life support, power and shielding, and keep the crew's body clocks in step with the Mars day. Not looking for new members.
summary:
Sol Shift is a free browser game for kids ages 7 to 12, built for Challenge #3, "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer." You run a small Mars base for 30 sols and keep three meters up: life support, power and shielding.

Every day you pick a work day or a rest day, and every choice costs something. Real solar flares and particle storms from NASA's DONKI records show up on the days they actually happened in May 2024, and you decide whether the crew hides in the storm shelter or keeps working. When you ask Earth for help, the answer comes back later.

The twist is sleep. A Mars day is about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day. If the crew keeps Earth hours, their body clocks slowly drift away from the Sun, they sleep worse, and tired people make more repair mistakes. NASA's own Phoenix mission team ran into this problem when they worked on Mars time.

The challenge asks for a game where a kid walks away understanding one real limit of living in deep space. Sol Shift's main lesson is the body clock, and along the way players also trade off life support, power and radiation shielding.
details:
What it does

You are in charge of a Mars base for 30 sols. A sol is one Mars day. Each sol has two parts.

1. Day. Sometimes a card comes first: a real solar event from NASA's records, a problem at the base (dusty solar panels, a water leak, a stuck rover), or an answer from Earth. Then you choose: Work day or Rest day. A work day fills the bars but tires the crew. A rest day lets the crew recover, but the base uses more than it makes, so the bars drop.

2. Night. Sometimes something goes wrong at night, like a pump that breaks at 3 a.m. Then you choose bedtime. Staying on Earth time is easy tonight, but the body clock slips about 40 minutes. Sleeping by the Sun is free while the clock is still in step. Once it has slipped, catching up costs one rough night.

The goal, "Keep all 3 bars above zero for 30 sols," stays on screen the whole game. Get through sol 30 and you win. If a meter hits zero, the mission ends. The end screen is a mission report that shows a chart of the three meters, what drained the one that ran out, and the real science behind it, with its source.

How a new player learns it

I played Sol Shift myself as a first-time player and found it confusing. There was too much on each screen and it wasn't clear what to do. This version is the fix.

- Each choice shows its result in plain words with small icons. The exact numbers are behind a "Show the numbers" switch, which is off by default, and "Real science" is folded until you open it.

- Short one-time tips introduce each part of the game the first time it shows up: the goal, the crew, a tired crew, a slipped body clock, a solar storm, asking Earth, and a low bar. The three "How to play" screens are still in the menu.

- The start is gentle. The bars start at 80, there are no random trouble cards in sols 1 to 5, a repair can't go wrong on sol 1, and solar storms hit the shield bar less than before.

No real kid has tested this new version yet.

How it connects to the challenge

- Life support, power and shielding. These are the three meters. The challenge page says two or three core resources work better for young players than five or six, so I kept it to three.

- Radiation shielding. On a flare or particle storm day, you choose between "Everyone into the storm shelter today" (safe, but no work gets done) and "Keep working outside" (more work, more risk).

- Food production. Greenhouse cards (new sprouts, broken grow lights, mold, and turning the greenhouse lights off to save power before a dust storm) make you trade food against power and crew time.

- Communication delay. Six cards let you "Ask Earth" instead of fixing something yourself. The answer arrives about one sol later. A real message takes about 4 to 24 minutes each way, but an answer also needs people on Earth to work out the fix. The game shows that wait as most of a day, and it doesn't claim that's the real signal time.

- No free choices. Every choice on all 23 cards costs something. A test checks this, because the challenge warns against a "safe" choice with no cost.

- Failure that teaches. When you lose, the mission report shows which meter ran out, what drained it, and the real science behind it. A new game starts right away.

How it works

- Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No server. You can even open it by double-clicking the file.

- The game rules sit in their own file, apart from the screen code, so they can be tested without a browser.

- Every number in the game is labeled in one data file as either a real-world fact (with its source link, checked on the source page) or a game-design number (a balance choice, not a NASA fact). The in-game Sources screen lists only the checked facts.

- The base, crew and ground are drawn with SVG shapes in code. Behind them are two real NASA photos taken by the Curiosity rover in Gale crater.

- Sound is off by default and made in code. People whose computers ask for reduced motion get no movement and no flashes. Low meters show a "Low" tag and a striped bar, so the warning never depends on color alone.

- Sleep is one module that can be switched off. With it off, the game still plays with the three meters, the real solar storms and the delayed answers from Earth.

How we tested the balance

A test script plays the real game engine with simple rule-following robot players written in code, 500 simulated games for each play style. Results on Nov 15, 2026:

Careful: rests a tired crew, sleeps by the Sun, shelters from big storms: 477 of 500 (95%)

Random clicker: presses any button, like a first-time player trying things: 173 of 500 (35%)

Careful, but always stays on Earth time: 138 of 500 (28%)

Careless: always works, stays on Earth time, never shelters: 0 of 500 (0%)

These are code robots, not people. Real players will differ, and testing with kids ages 7 to 12 is the next step.

Benefits and goals

- Kids learn three real things by playing: a Mars day is longer than an Earth day, radiation is a daily cost on Mars, and help from Earth is never instant.

- It's free and runs on a school Chromebook, a phone or a library computer.

- The words are written for ages 7 to 12. Terms like "sol," "radiation dose" and "solar flare" are explained right where they show up, and one-time tips teach each part of the game the first time it appears.

- Teachers can add a new event by copying one block in one file.

Tools and languages

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG and the Web Audio API in the browser. Node.js runs the balance tests. Python scripts rebuild the NASA data snapshot and the photo crops. The Orbitron font is used under the SIL Open Font License. Git was used for version control.
